Abakinnyi ba filimi bo muri Hollywood, Brad Pitt na Angelina Jolie, bumvikanye kurangiza amakimbirane y'amategeko yari amaze igihe hagati yabo ajyanye no kugurisha imigabane ya Jolie mu ruganda rwabo rwa divayi rwo mu Bufaransa.

Aya makimbirane yavutse mu gihe aba bombi, bari mu nzira zo gutandukana.

Mu itangazo bahuriyemo, ababahagarariye bagize bati: "Twumvikanye hanze y'urukiko mu nyungu z'umuryango wacu, kandi nta bindi bisobanuro tuzatanga kuri iki kibazo."

Pitt na Jolie baguze imigabane ibaha ububasha bwo kugenzura uruganda rwa divayi rwa Château Miraval mu mwaka wa 2008, nyuma baza no kuhakorera ubukwe bwabo mu 2014.

Mu rubanza, Pitt w'imyaka 62 yavugaga ko Jolie w'imyaka 51 yagurishije umugabane we wo muri urwo ruganda rw'inzoga atabanje kumugisha inama, ndetse akawugurisha ku muherwe w'Uburusiya Yuri Shefler.

Jolie na we, yareze Pitt, amushinja ko yamukoreye ihohoterwa ndetse akanahutaza bamwe mu bana babo mu rugendo rw'indege rwabaye mu 2016, ibintu yavuze ko byatumye asaba gatanya.

Amasezerano yatangajwe ku wa gatatu arangiza ibyo birego byombi.

Mu itangazo ryatanzwe n'ababahagarariye, bongeyeho ko: "Ibivugwa mu binyamakuru, ndetse bakemeza ko byaturutse ku bantu bafite amakuru y'imbere, ntabwo biba biturutse kuri twe cyangwa ku bantu batwegereye."

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Mu kirego cya Pitt, yashinjaga Jolie gushaka kumugirira nabi igihe yagurishaga umugabane we muri Château Miraval, kandi ko ibyo byatumye asigara akorana n'"umuntu atazi ufite imikorere n'intego mbi."

Uyu mukinnyi wamamaye muri filimi Fight Club yavugaga ko we n'uwahoze ari umugore we, bari barumvikanye ko nta n'umwe wagurisha imigabane ye muri urwo ruganda atabanje kubimenyesha no kubyemeranywaho n'undi.

Ku ruhande rwa Jolie, na we yareze Pitt amushinja kumujegeza umutwe no gukubita abana babo babiri, ubwo bari mu rugendo rw'indege bwite mu 2016.

Yanavugaga ko Pitt yatutse abagize umuryango we ndetse akabasukaho inzoga muri urwo rugendo rwari ruvuye mu Bufaransa rujya i Los Angeles muri Amerika.

Abunganira Jolie mu mategeko, bavuze ko Pitt yatangiye gutaka cyane ashinja umugore we guha abana babo batandatu ubwisanzure bukabije. Icyo gihe abo bana bari bafite hagati y'imyaka umunani na 15.

Nyuma y'iperereza rya polisi kuri ibyo birego, Pitt ntiyigeze akurikiranwa mu nkiko kandi yahakanye ibyo yashinjwaga byose.

Mu mpera z'umwaka ushize, Pitt na Jolie bumvikanye kuri gatanya yabo, bishyira iherezo ku rugamba rw'amategeko rwari rumaze imyaka umunani.

Gusa amakuru avuga ko urubanza Pitt afitanye na Stoli Group, sosiyete ikora ibinyobwa ifitwe n'umukungu Yuri Shefler, wanaguze imigabane ya Angelina Jolie, rwo rugikomeje.

Igihe bashyingiranwaga mu 2014, Pitt na Jolie bari bamwe mu bantu bakomeye kandi binjiza amafaranga menshi kurusha abandi muri Hollywood.

Bahuriye mu ikorwa rya filimi Mr and Mrs Smith mu 2005, maze ibitangazamakuru bibaha izina rya "Brangelina", rikomoka ku mazina yabo yombi.

Bakibana bagiraga igihe bagashaka abana bava mu miryango ifite ibibazo, cyangwa se bariho mu buzima bubi maze bakabarera byemewe n'amategeko ndetse bakanabiyandikishaho.

Kuva batandukana, amakuru yanditse mu nkiko agaragaza ko abana bane muri batandatu bahinduye amazina yabo y'umuryango, bakoresha Jolie gusa aho gukoresha Jolie-Pitt.

MN202611_6o2es2ye5s.t:
Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash

It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.

"I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.

Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City , Chelsea , Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving .

A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving.

His Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.

He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".

So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?

Footage was released of the footballer driving dangerously

Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.

It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.

This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter , external .

Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.

It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.

According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16–24 years.

It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.

This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.

BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.

Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.

He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release.

"I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added.

"It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing."

Broughton said he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.

"I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added.

"I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it."

Broughton has developed an app to help tackle issues with mental health and under-performance in football.

He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.

But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.

"I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he said.

BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.

Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', said a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.

She said: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon.

"So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.

"Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days.

"So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up."

Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha said more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.

Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley.

"Look at what's happened to Raheem," he said. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time.

"But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's important to support people who have issues with nitrous oxide."

The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.

"I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he said.

"Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking.

"The players are doing it, but it's more sophisticated in terms of how they do it, the locations, and this is an example here with nitrous oxide."

Neurologist Dr Nicholl has been working with patients who have abused nitrous oxide for years and issued a warning to others.

"It certainly is being used by footballers, but it's pretty much the worst thing that you want to be using if you're a professional sportsperson," he said.

"It damages your spinal cord and the spinal cord is a bit like an electrical cable, where the insulation - the outside of that cable - gets stripped away.

"So what patients will complain of is difficulty with feeling on their hands or feet, or unable to walk at all.

"So, in effect, it's like a spinal cord injury. But they can also get blood clots, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and some patients have died."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

MN202611_qx20e4uwuy.t:
James Dean Bradfield said their rock songs about banking, environmental damage and ideology still have relevance today after three decades

Manic Street Preachers frontman James Dean Bradfield said playing in Wales brings "extra pressure" as the band prepare to mark 35 years of their debut album.

The band will headline Blackweir Fields in Cardiff next summer, performing the landmark 1992 record Generation Terrorists in full.

Bradfield said their rock songs about banking, environmental damage and ideology still "have a prescience for anything you could talk about now".

He said when the band wrote the album, which sold 250,000 copies worldwide upon its release, they were "a bit unreasonable and a bit mad" but also "fiercely ambitious".

Bradfield, raised in Blackwood, Caerphilly, said the album was shaped by the decline of the south Wales valleys after pit closures, channeling their surroundings into songs such as Nat West-Barclays-Midlands-Lloyds, Slash N Burn and Crucifix Kiss.

While discussing Nat West-Barclays-Midlands-Lloyds, he said: "That song has a prescient nature about it and it always will.

"Even though it dates itself, you can take some of the songs and you can actually trace them over the times that we live in now."

Bradfield joked that he and his band mates Nicky Wire, Sean Moore and the late Richey Edwards were "fun to hang out with, I promise you".

Sean Moore, James Dean Bradfield and Nicky Wire have been a three-piece lineup since 1995. Their forth band member Richey Edwards disappeared in February of that year

The album also features Little Baby Nothing, which Bradfield originally envisioned Kylie Minogue singing.

"She did sing on stage with us once in the Shepherd's Bush Empire. I think that was during the Everything Must Go tour, and she was brilliant," he said.

Previously, Bradfield translated one of their songs from their fifth album, This Is My Truth Tell Me Yours, into Welsh for a S4C music series.

"It was a challenge to sing Ready for Drowning in Welsh, definitely," he said.

"I tried to do the lyrics justice in Welsh as much as it had been done justice in English.

"I tried to keep it as poetic as possible rather than just the facts."

Fans told to expect Nicky Wire "to really be rocking the leopard print more than you could imagine"

Bradfield said playing at home in Wales was "a privilege" but came with "more pressure" than gigs elsewhere.

"You can't hide away from the fact that there's more pressure and there's a lot more tension around a hometown gig.

"All those pressures add into making it, it feels like there's more at stake.

"You might see people on the dog walk that came to the concert the night before," he said, laughing.

"You don't want them to give you a bad review when you're getting a coffee with your dog."

He also admitted that he sometimes worries about the prospect of family members being in the crowd and swearing on stage.

"One of my uncles or aunties are going to be in the crowd and I better watch my language. And you're thinking, what am I talking about? I'm in a band," he said.

Asked which songs younger fans should start with, Bradfield picked Crucifix Kiss, Nat West-Barclays-Midlands-Lloyds and So Dead, a song they have never played live.

"Those three songs in themselves, I think, still have a prescience for anything you could talk about now."

L-R Richey Edwards, James Dean Bradfield, Nicky Wire and Sean Moore

Discussing their one-night performance in June 2027, Bradfield said he felt "nervous" about playing the full album and had already started rehearsing.

"I think they can expect a band that's very, very tight, pretty aggressive, but we're going to be on message in terms of the record that we're representing."

He added: "It's going to be very faithful."

Bradfield told fans to expect Wire "to really be rocking the leopard print more than you could imagine."

The Libertines, The Cardigans and The Tub will be supporting the band on Saturday 19 June 2027.

He added: "We've got to try and find a way to honour Richey as well."

Edwards, from Blackwood, disappeared on 1 February 1995.

His car was found abandoned near the old Severn Bridge , but no trace of him has ever been found, and he was declared legally dead in 2008.

MN202611_hsi0bvawsp.t:
Paul Whitehouse said the government "needs to act now"

Comedian and TV presenter Paul Whitehouse has called for the government to help save an at-risk fish species present in England's largest lake since the end of the last Ice Age.

Windermere, in the Lake District, has been home to Arctic charr for more than 10,000 years, but campaigners warn extinction beckons as the fish's habitat is harmed by sewage pollution, invasive species competing for food and rising temperatures caused by global warming.

Whitehouse urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to act and said it would be "a crime" if the species were lost.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it shared "the public's determination to protect this iconic lake".

Whitehouse, who fronts the BBC's Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing series alongside fellow comedian Bob Mortimer, said the "spawning grounds for this beautiful species are covered in algal sludge that is a direct result of sewage pollution".

"This government needs to act now," he added.

Arctic charr have been described as a "living link to the end of the last Ice Age"

The former Fast Show star is helping environmental campaigner Matt Staniek unveil a 1.3m (5ft 6in) ice sculpture depicting the prime minister outside No 10 North, in Manchester, to highlight the fish's plight.

Staniek wants the prime minister to expedite a £3.7bn scheme that would include a huge tunnel carrying sewage to a new state-of-the-art water treatment works .

It has been drawn up by the Only Rainwater In Windermere coalition comprising United Utilities (UU), the Environment Agency, Lake District National Park Authority (LDNPA), the Love Windermere partnership, Save Windermere campaign group and Westmorland and Furness Council.

It comes as new research from the Freshwater Biological Association (FBA) also warns Arctic charr are in serious decline and face extinction in the lake without "urgent action".

The fish, which is genetically distinct from Arctic charr in the region's other lakes, lives in four separate populations in Windermere that spawn at different times of year and different places and do not interbreed.

The FBA said spawning habitat quality had "declined markedly" at Windermere since 2017 with levels of silt and algae increasing while introduced species, such as ruffe, roach and bream, were "on the rise".

Windermere has long been popular with visitors but it faces a number of pressures, campaigners say

Dr Louise Lavictoire, the organisation's head of science, said the research had "shown very clearly that we are at risk of losing Arctic charr from Windermere completely".

"The species is facing multiple pressures and research gives us the evidence, data and sense of urgency to take collective action to protect this ancient fish species before it's too late."

The research was funded by groups including Natural England, the Environment Agency and the LDNPA.

Natural England's Dave Ottewell described Arctic charr as "remarkable fish" and a "living link to the end of the last Ice Age".

Tim Duckmanton, team leader for strategy and environment at the LDNPA, echoed that sentiment and said "thanks to data collected, we now have a better understanding of threats to the species".

UU, which manages infrastructure around the lake, said protecting the area was a "priority" and that £200m was being invested over the next four years in an effort to cut spills from storm overflows and improve wastewater treatment.

A Defra spokesperson said: "This government is already acting to reduce sewage discharges, including deploying 33 additional Environment Agency specialists in the region, increasing inspections and through our regional water council's giving the local community in Windermere a greater say in decision making.

"Our strengthened Water Bill will bring in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment."

MN202611_1sii0asawrm.t:
Dozens of people were killed in August after a rubbish landfill collapsed in Conakry

Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.

Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday announced a deadline of 31 December to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.

In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.

The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.

At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.

He said much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.

The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs.

"The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said.

"Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.

He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.

Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a new disposal site in Baretodé, outside the capital.

The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.

The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.

According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

MN202611_1tugnzv8leh.t:
Referees rely on the opinions of former players to determine a significant part of their annual salary

It has become something of a Wednesday morning ritual for fans. At 10am, the Premier League releases the latest votes of its Key Match Incidents Panel.

For four seasons, the KMI Panel was a clandestine operation. It was distributed to clubs only, but it would still find its way out into the public domain.

This season, it began being released to the public.

Yet little is really understood about the KMI Panel.

Why does it exist? Is it just protecting referees? And does it really mean anything?

For referees, the last question is more important than you might realise.

The votes, which ultimately say whether referees have got a decision right or wrong, create a merit table of performance - and this impacts their salary.

"It depends where you are on the list," former Premier League referee Graham Scott said. "But if you're in the middle, then it might be 25% of your take-home. So it's substantial."

For the officials, these are not decisions being taken by their bosses.

Their performance reviews are effectively outsourced to a group of former players.

The results can be inconsistent and frustrating as much for the referees as they are for the fans.

Let's take a look at how a referee's salary works in the Premier League.

A Premier League official will earn , on average, about £175,000 per year. The scale will run between £125,000 and £250,000.

Think that is unduly high? Referees in Spain's La Liga are the highest paid in the world, according to Marca, with an average yearly salary of £221,000.

Premier League officials are about on par with those in the German Bundesliga and Italian Serie A.

In England, there is a guaranteed base wage of 50%. This will differ depending on the seniority and experience of an official.

Michael Oliver would be at the top of the bracket, a newcomer like Farai Hallam at the other end.

The other 50% is based upon a set of variables, with match fees a major part.

Each on-field appointment is worth a little over £1000, with a VAR game slightly less.

Last season, Anthony Taylor refereed the most Premier League games, 31, followed by Chris Kavanagh, 30, and Michael Oliver, 29.

Kavanagh and Oliver worked as VAR on a handful of occasions, while Taylor did not do any.

Stuart Attwell had the most combined appointments at 52, with 25 games as a referee and 27 as a VAR.

Finally, there is the subjective element - the KMI Panel.

The votes determine the annual bonus payments for all officials.

Until 2022, referees' body Pro Ref, or PGMOL as it was known until this summer, used to do its own assessment of its referees' decisions.

But clubs grew restless, feeling referees were marking their own homework.

It is made up of five members. Three are former players and coaches, plus there is a representative for the Premier League and one for Pro Ref.

Their identities remain secret, with the former professionals selected from a pool on rotation.

What you won't see on the published version is that each incident is given a difficulty rating, ranging from one to five, which is taken into account when drawing up the referees' merit table.

All this really is, of course, is another layer of subjectivity. On top of the referees, VAR, players and coaches.

"People complain about the consistency of referees on field, of VAR interventions, or otherwise," said Scott, who now acts as the refereeing expert for the Athletic.

"But then, if you look at the KMI Panel outcomes, they're also inconsistent."

It is a view shared by Andy Davies, who retired as a Championship referee last year.

"Naturally, there will always be a level of interest given as it provides a significant part of income for the season," Davies said.

"But ultimately, the KMI Panel lacks any real credibility amongst referees."

Graham Scott was a Premier League referee for 10 years and acted as a VAR for more than 100 matches

Referees are scored on their on-field decision-making. If an error has been corrected by the VAR, it still counts as a mistake for the merit table.

Those at the top of the table will be rewarded well, while those at the bottom are not likely to receive much of a bonus payment at all.

Let's take a look at the numbers from last season.

Michael Oliver was the top referee, getting 93.5% of KMIs correct. John Brooks, Darren England and Simon Hooper were very marginally behind.

For other referees, the borderline decisions, ones which are the most subjective and sit in the grey areas, can be an issue.

One vote could be the difference between a referee being right or wrong. And a place on the merit table, impacting how much they get paid.

Last season, Sam Barrott and Jarred Gillett were both told they made four errors to a 2:3 vote.

Attwell, meanwhile, had three of the more high-profile incidents go in his favour to a 3:2 vote.

"The ones that sit in the margins can be very contentious and inconsistent," said Scott.

"You think, well, how can that be right? You know, that's not definitive, is it? It could have gone either way.

"But there seems to be a reluctance to allow that 'seen them given' sort of mentality, neither right nor wrong.

"Relying on such a small group of people to be so definitive, especially when they vote 3:2, is unhealthy and unhelpful."

As well as determining the merit table for each referee's salary, what the KMI Panel says can guide how games are refereed.

The members of the KMI Panel can be influenced by public opinion, and inconsistency means referees are often having to change the way they approach games, only to be told it is wrong.

"I have spoken to many referees, even this season," Davies said. "And they have no idea which way the panel is going to fall at times, or which way Pro Ref are going to vote because of how political it can be."

Scott used the example of holding when an attacker is offside.

In December last year, Brentford 's Dango Ouattara was pulled back against Leeds . The penalty was cancelled by the VAR for offside. The KMI Panel voted 5:0 it was correct.

Last month, Arsenal were not given a penalty against Hull , when an offside Kai Havertz was pulled back by Nobel Mendy. The KMI Panel voted 5:0 it was incorrect.

"One minute we're told football expects an offside," Scott said. "Okay, we'll deliver that for you. We do it again, and they say the opposite.

"Referees get confused on the back of that mixed feedback. It just shows how the system's flawed.

"The game can afford to invest more in this process, and a properly independent approach."

For now, at least, referees have no choice but to rely on the KMI Panel to determine a chunk of their salary.

MN202611_tc2pw2unao.t:
Portuguese second-tier side Torreense have not played top-flight football since the 1991-92 campaign, but are making their debut in the Europa League this season

S.C.U Torreense's league fixtures this season include meetings with the 'B' teams of Sporting, Benfica and Porto.

But the Portuguese second division club, located 35 miles north of Lisbon, are in this season's Europa League after stunning giants Sporting to win the Taca de Portugal in May.

"This is a landmark moment," Andre Sabino, the club's director of football and CEO told BBC Sport.

Torreense had never played a European home match before their 2-1 defeat by Sunderland in October and welcome Celtic to Leiria on Thursday (20:00 GMT).

They won at Norwegian side Lillestrom on their debut but lost heavily in Hungary against Ferencvaros before beating Ararat-Armenia last time out.

Managed by Luis Tralhao, whose brother Joao is an assistant to Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, the club are hoping to do more than just make up the numbers.

"It is something extraordinary for Torreense. These are clubs with huge histories, strong identities and enormous European experience," Sabino added.

"To be able to share the same competition and compete against them is a privilege. But we don't want to simply participate. We want to compete."

Torreense captain and Cape Verde international Stopira (pictured above) scored a penalty in extra time as his side beat Sporting 2-1 in the Taca de Portugal final earlier this year

Second-tier Beira-Mar played in the 1999-2000 Uefa Cup, although they were a top-flight team at the time of qualifying. But Torreense are the first team from the second division to qualify by winning the Taca de Portugal.

"The Portuguese Cup has been played since 1938 in its current model and it was the first time that a second division team won it," Portuguese football journalist and ex-Benfica goalkeeper Jose Delgado told BBC Sport.

"You can imagine when they could defeat a giant club like Sporting in the final, it was quite a surprise and for the city, it's something very, very special."

After beating Lillestrom, they have already exceeded the expectations of some. "I thought that Torreense could go through the Europa League with no points," added Delgado.

With Portugal ranked outside Uefa's top five leagues, every club in the Champions League, Europa League or Conference League has a responsibility to perform well to earn their nation important ranking points.

"For Portuguese football, everybody [thought it] was nice that a club like Torreense won the cup but also we had some concerns," said Delgado.

"The first game everybody thought that Torreense had no chance against Lillestrom and they won. It was quite a good surprise. But it's like a fairytale for Torreense because they are a small club."

Torreense's Estadio Manuel Marques has a capacity smaller than 45 of the 48 clubs in England's sixth tier

As their 2,431-capacity home at Estadio Manuel Marques does not pass Uefa's stadium criteria, they will instead face Celtic almost 47 miles away at the Municipal Stadium in Leiria.

"Obviously, it is not ideal," Sabino explained. "Playing at home should mean playing in your own stadium, in front of your own supporters and in the environment that represents your club.

"But at the same time, we understand the logistical and regulatory requirements involved in European competition.

"We have to look at the bigger picture. We are extremely grateful for the opportunity to compete in the Europa League and we will make Leiria feel as much like home as possible."

The additional travel has not deterred supporters from watching their beloved club face big European names.

"Our supporters and our people are what make a home, regardless of the kilometres. The response from our supporters has been fantastic," Sabino added.

"They understand that this is a historic moment for Torreense and they want to experience it with us.

"We hope to see Leiria filled with Torreense colours and feel that support from the first minute."

Torreense pocketed 630,000 euros (£533,000) for their win over Lillestrom

Torreense missed out on a return to Portugal's top division for the first time since 1991-92 after a 2-0 two-legged defeat by Casa Pia in a promotion/relegation play-off in May. And fell at the first hurdle in their defence of the Taca de Portugal.

But qualification for the Europa League's league phase guarantees a financial injection of at least 5m euros (£4.2m).

Every positive result and extra round reached adds more to that pot.

"For a club like Torreense, it is a very significant amount," Sabino explained. "It gives us an opportunity to strengthen the club in several areas and to accelerate projects that otherwise would naturally take much longer.

"However, we have to be very responsible. Success can create opportunities but it also creates responsibilities.

"Our objective is not simply to spend more because we have more resources. We want to invest intelligently, strengthen the structure of the club and create conditions for sustainable growth."

Torreense played competitively against Sporting's main and 'B' teams last season, something they will also do this year against Porto

Torreense have made 19 new signings from across the globe for this season.

As well as turning to Portugal's top flight for five new recruits, other signings have come from France, Greece, Spain, Serbia, Portugal, Brazil, Denmark, Morocco and Germany. The majority from outside those countries' top leagues.

Of their 32-man senior squad, just four are Portuguese.

"It has been a very different challenge," Sabino explained. "European football changes the perception of the club and naturally makes Torreense more attractive to certain players, but it also increases expectations."

Last season, Torreense missed out on automatic promotion on goal difference before losing the play-off. This term they have won only two of their opening 10 league games and sit 13th.

With the overwhelming majority of football fans in Portugal supporting one of the 'big three' of Porto, Benfica and Sporting - Delgado says sometimes home fans even cheer for their more illustrious opponents when they visit.

"Right now I think that there is a great sympathy about Torreense, but I don't think they will get many more [fans] because of this presence," he added.

"Maybe this presence will make some investors look at them in a different way and put some money in the club."

MN202611_1sxcoyu5lfo.t:
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba's social media posts have previously sparked diplomatic tensions

The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.

In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.

The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.

The Ugandan government has yet to respond.

The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.

Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.

Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.

Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever

The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter

In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahema ethnic community.

The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.

They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.

He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.

Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.

Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.

It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.

During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."

The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels , with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.

Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.

"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.

"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".

The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".

It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.

In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.

In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.

The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.

In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

Umunya-Canada utwara ibyogajuru, ari mu byishimo nyuma yo kwibaruka umwana we wa gatatu, n'ubwo we n'isi batandukanyijwe n'ibirometero amamiliyoni.

Ikigo cy'Igihugu cya Canada gishinzwe iby'isanzure (Canadian Space Agency) cyatangaje ku wa kabiri ko Joshua Kutryk n'umugore we Heather Kutryk bibarutse umwana w'umukobwa, mu gihe Joshua ari mu rugendo rw'amezi atandatu rwo mu isanzure rwatangiye mu kwezi k'ukwakira (10).

Mu itangazo ryashyizwe ahagaragara n'iki kigo, abo bombi bagize bati: "N'ubwo hagati yacu harimo iirometero byinshi, twumva dukomeje kuba hamwe cyane mu gihe twakiriye aka kana kacu gashya mu muryango."

Uyu mugabo uri mu rugendo rwe rwa mbere rwo mu isanzure, ni umuntu wa kane gusa mu mateka wabaye kure y'umuryango we mu gihe umwana we yavukaga, na we, ari kuri sitasiyo mpuzamahanga yo mu kirere.

Joshua na Heather basanzwe bafite abandi bana babiri bafite imyaka itanu n'irindwi.

Bagize bati: "Twishimiye cyane ko umuryango wacu ugenda waguka kandi dutegerezanyije amatsiko igihe twese uko turi batanu tuzongera guhura."

Bavuze kandi ko uru rugendo rwa Joshua rwari inzozi yari yaragize kuva akiri umwana.

Bagize bati: "Turifuza kwereka abana bacu ko inzozi zikomeye zikwiye gukurikiranwa, ko gukora cyane no kudacika intege bifite akamaro, kandi ko iyo umuntu ashyigikiwe n'umuryango n'abamukikije ashobora kugera ku bidasanzwe."

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Mbere yo gutwara ibyogajuru, Joshua Kutryk ukomoka mu mujyi wa Fort Saskatchewan mu ntara ya Alberta, yari umupilote w'indege z'intambara ndetse afite ipeti rya koloneli mu ngabo zirwanira mu kirere za Canada.

Yinjijwe muri Canadian Space Agency mu mwaka wa 2017.

Kutryk ni we Munya-Canada rukumbi watoranyijwe mu butumwa bwa NASA na SpaceX bwiswe Crew-13, burimo gukorerwamo ubushakashatsi bwa siyansi ndetse hakanageragerezwa ikoranabuhanga rishya mu isanzure.

Iryo tsinda rigizwe kandi n'Abanyamerika babiri, Luke Delaney na Jessica Watkins, hamwe n'Umurusiya umwe, Sergey Teteryatnikov.

Mbere y'uko bahaguruka tariki ya mbere Ukwakira(10), Heather Kutryk yabwiye radiyo na televiziyo bya Canada, CBC News, ko umuryango wabo wari umaze imyaka myinshi witegura uru rugendo kuko rwari rumaze igihe rutegerejwe.

Yavuze kandi ko inda yari atwite itari yarateguwe mbere ariko ko yabaye "ikintu cyiza cyane".

Ati: "Ntabwo mfite impungenge nyinshi. Dufite abantu benshi badushyigikiye. Nitaweho cyane na CSA na NASA."

Yongeyeho ati: "Ni amezi atandatu gusa, ndizera ko bizagenda neza."

Mu kiganiro cyihariye Joshua Kutryk yagiranye na CBS News, yavuze ko yifuza ko umwana we wavutse adahari, azakura abona ko se yemeye kugira ibyo yigomwa no gufata ingorane zimwe na zimwe ku bw'inyungu rusange n'umurimo wo gukorera igihugu cye cya Canada.

Central Bank Governor Soraya Hakuziyaremye with other Bank officials at the MPC press conference on Thursday

The National Bank of Rwanda (BNR) has raised its Central Bank Rate (CBR) from 8.75% to 9.5%, an increase of 75 basis points, stepping up efforts to contain inflation that has continued to rise despite earlier monetary policy tightening.

Governor Soraya Hakuziyaremye announced the decision on Thursday, November 26, following a meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which reviewed domestic and international economic developments and their implications for price stability.

The increase comes as Rwanda faces mounting inflationary pressures, particularly from food prices, which have pushed the cost of living higher for households.

Annual headline inflation averaged 15.8% in the third quarter of 2026, up from 13.2% in the previous quarter, before climbing further to 19.5% in October, according to the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR).

Fresh food prices have been a major contributor to the increase. In October, they were 39.9% higher than a year earlier, while the overall food and non-alcoholic beverages category recorded an annual increase of 28.9%.

Core inflation, which excludes fresh food and energy prices, stood at 11.5%, indicating that price pressures have extended beyond the more volatile food and energy categories.

The central bank aims to maintain inflation within a target range of 2% to 8%, with a medium-term objective of 5%.

Raising the Central Bank Rate is one of the main tools available to BNR to influence borrowing costs and control the amount of money circulating in the economy.

A higher policy rate generally pushes up interest rates charged by commercial banks, making loans more expensive for households and businesses. This can reduce borrowing and spending, helping to slow demand and ease pressure on prices.

The effects also extend to money markets. Rwanda’s interbank rate averaged 8.44% in the third quarter of 2026, compared with 5.85% during the same period last year, reflecting the impact of tighter monetary conditions.

However, higher interest rates can also increase financing costs for businesses, potentially slowing investment and economic activity.

The monetary tightening comes against a backdrop of strong economic growth.

Rwanda’s economy expanded by 9.4% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, supported mainly by services and industry.

The challenge for monetary authorities is therefore to bring inflation under control without undermining the country’s economic growth momentum.

BNR expects inflation to begin easing progressively from the second quarter of 2027, returning to its target range by the end of that year.

The outlook remains exposed to several risks, including adverse weather conditions that could disrupt agricultural production and push food prices higher.

The bank also identified geopolitical tensions in the Middle East as a potential source of further increases in international energy and commodity prices.

The Monetary Policy Committee said it would continue monitoring domestic and global economic developments and take further action where necessary to bring inflation sustainably back towards its medium-term target.

MN202611_1tnsv01lrgv.t:
The 2026 event was held in Sunderland's Herrington Country Park

BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend is heading to Brighton for 2027, it has been announced.

The annual music festival will take place in Preston Park from Friday 28 to Sunday 30 May next year.

Radio 1 Breakfast Show host Greg James told listeners he is "so excited" to bring the festival to the city as he revealed the news on air, adding: "It's going to be amazing".

Tens of thousands of fans are expected to attend the three-day event, which will feature about 70 acts, from some of the biggest names in music to new emerging artists.

Big Weekend, BBC Radio 1's flagship event, is held in a new location each year - often in towns and cities that don't get as many big live music events.

In previous years acts such as US pop star Taylor Swift came to Norwich and Swansea, grime star Stormzy performed in Exeter, pop rock band The 1975 headlined in Dundee and US singer Bruno Mars featured in Londonderry.

Breakfast host Greg said: "If Radio 1 was a place, it would be Brighton.

"It's got an amazing musical heritage, loves bringing different people together and wants to make sure fun is prioritised.

"It's actually stupid that it's taken so long for us to do a Big Weekend there. Sorry about that."

Last year the event was held in Sunderland's Herrington Country Park, where about 100,000 music fans basked in the the sun while dancing to a host of major artists.

Grammy and Brit Awards winner Olivia Dean, Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and veteran DJ Fatboy Slim topped the bill across the weekend.

Irish star CMAT, Messy singer Lola Young, former One Directioner Niall Horan and American singer Kehlani were also on the line-up.

The vibrancy of the current electronic music scene led Radio 1 to dedicate day one of Big Weekend to its Dance Party brand for the first time.

It spanned styles, backgrounds and generations - with local lad Max Jones getting the party started on the Introducing stage, and Fisher, MK and Clementine Douglas keeping the party going throughout the day.

Big Weekend tickets are usually significantly cheaper than most major festivals, with a proportion reserved for local residents.

It has not yet been revealed when tickets will go on sale for the 2027 event and at what price.

MN202611_1j2oaj2h6zw.t:
Pakistan's Dar-e-Nijaat TV show has become a sensation in India

Until Wednesday, the weekend plans of some television enthusiasts in the Indian city of Bengaluru involved dressing up, having an elaborate dinner and finding out what happens next in the lives of a wildly popular fictional Pakistani couple.

Two private screenings of Dar-e-Nijaat (Door to Salvation), a Pakistani television drama that has become something of a sensation on Indian social media, were called off after an online backlash and police scrutiny.

The serial, which airs on Pakistan's ARY Digital, is available to Indian viewers through some YouTube channels, though the broadcaster's official channel is blocked in India.

The controversy comes amid a renewed appetite for Pakistani entertainment in India, even though cultural engagement remains a sensitive issue following a brief but intense military confrontation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours in May last year.

A similar gathering in Delhi, featuring quizzes and even a virtual interaction with the show's director, had already divided opinion online last week.

In Bengaluru, one screening, scheduled for Saturday at a restaurant, offered a Persian and Arabic dinner alongside two episodes of the serial for a small ticket charge. The other - scheduled at a private theatre and meant only for family members - asked guests to dress in their "best Pakistani ensemble".

As promotional posters circulated online, several social media users questioned the appropriateness of such gatherings and called for police intervention. Both events have since been called off.

The backlash has coincided with calls to block the release of another Pakistani drama in India.

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi demanding that Netflix's upcoming Pakistani series, Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo (Gather whatever is left), be barred from release in India.

Featuring Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan, Sanam Saeed and other stars with many Indian fans, the series is Pakistan's first Netflix original. Its global premiere is scheduled for 4 December.

In its letter to Modi on Tuesday, the AICWA argued that releasing the series in India would disregard the sentiments of families affected by terrorism. India has long accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, an allegation Islamabad denies.

One of the event invitations asked guests to dress in Pakistani attire

The association has also sought permanent legislation prohibiting Pakistani entertainment content in India. Netflix is yet to clarify whether the series will be available to Indian subscribers.

The developments have revived an old debate in India over whether cultural ties with Pakistan should be kept separate from political differences.

India and Pakistan share a rich cultural heritage, but relations between them have often been fraught since they were carved out of British India as independent nations in 1947.

And cultural exchanges have often been among the first casualties of political tensions. Pakistani ghazal singers with devoted audiences in India have periodically found themselves unable to perform there. Indian films, immensely popular in Pakistan, have disappeared from its cinemas. Artistic collaborations have flourished during periods of relative calm, only to unravel when tensions flare again .

The early 2010s were a particularly fertile period. Pakistani singers Atif Aslam and Rahat Fateh Ali Khan were among the most recognisable voices in Hindi cinema. The launch of the television channel Zindagi in 2014 brought Pakistani serials into Indian living rooms, introducing viewers to stories whose language and emotional worlds were familiar, but whose treatment of everyday life often felt refreshingly different.

By 2016, Fawad Khan was appearing in some of Bollywood's most prominent productions. But attacks on Indian security forces in Uri that year and in Pulwama in 2019, both of which India blamed on Pakistan-based militant groups, narrowed the space for cultural collaboration. Pakistan - which has constantly denied any involvement - also imposed restrictions on Indian entertainment.

Even as formal exchanges dwindled, Pakistani dramas found new audiences in India on YouTube, while music continued to travel across the border through streaming platforms.

But the events of last year disrupted even this relatively informal relationship.

Pakistani actor Fawad Khan has starred in a few Bollywood films and has many fans in India

On 22 April 2025, militants killed 26 people, most of them tourists , in Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan-linked militants; Islamabad denied involvement. In May, India launched military strikes on what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Four days of fighting followed before a ceasefire was announced.

Amid widespread anger in India, the government asked streaming platforms to discontinue Pakistani-origin content, while social media accounts of several Pakistani celebrities were blocked.

Fawad Khan's much-anticipated return to Hindi cinema with Abir Gulaal was thwarted when the film was denied permission for release in India. Criticism of India's military action by Pakistani artistes fuelled further anger.

For much of the past year, Indian audiences have encountered Pakistan on screen largely through the prism of national security. In December, millions flocked to watch Dhurandhar , Aditya Dhar's espionage thriller, whose success inspired a fascination with the gangsters, spies and political intrigues of Karachi.

But in recent months, a more familiar kind of fascination with Pakistan has begun to resurface.

Pakistani songs like Alfaaz have become hugely popular on Indian social media, while Dar-e-Nijaat, a story about marriage, heartbreak and domestic life, has found an enthusiastic audience.

Written by the celebrated Urdu novelist Umera Ahmed, the serial revolves around the marriage of Zaryab (Durefishan Saleem), a young woman recovering from a romantic betrayal, and Abu Bakar (Sheheryar Munawar), a deeply religious man.

Though the drama explores questions of faith and redemption, it is Abu Bakar's tenderness towards his wife that has earned him perhaps the highest accolade in the contemporary vocabulary of courtship: a "green flag".

It was this enthusiasm for the drama that prompted the organiser of one of the screenings in Bengaluru to plan an event at a private theatre in her apartment complex.

What she had envisaged as a small family gathering, she said, had been interpreted quite differently once the invitation found its way onto X.

"My family was saying why should we cancel?" she said. But ultimately, she decided to call it off.

MN202611_92vgq2od6w.t:
Twin sisters Romina (left) and Taraneh Rahimi were arrested in late January, their cousin says

In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.

She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.

He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.

He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.

Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.

January's protests began over economic grievances and spread to become Iran's largest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution

The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".

The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

Taraneh loves horses and would like to set up her own breeding centre one day, her cousin says

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.

Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".

Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.

This image of Mahboubeh Shabani, sentenced to death in September, has been shared with human rights groups

Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.

Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.

"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.

The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.

The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."

Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, rights groups say

Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".

At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".

Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".

Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".

In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".

Taraneh (left) and Romina both say they gave baseless confessions after being tortured

Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.

Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."

Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.

Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.

Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.

Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.

Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

MN202611_18nabnl384f.t:
Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter

A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.

Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled)

At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.

There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.

In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."

It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.

French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.

The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.

While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".

Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.

In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.

In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.

Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.

News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.

He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cans

The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.

Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.

The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.

"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.

Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.

Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.

On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.

The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police

Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.

Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.

The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.

We confronted Marvin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules

When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.

He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.

It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.

The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.

Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor" . However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.

The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

MN202611_17tmvkm3iyc.t:
Rwanda has entered a difficult international debate after French MP Prisca Thevenot questioned plans to accommodate some migrants in the country. Foreign Affairs Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe rejected her description of the proposed facilities as “camps.”

He pointed to Rwanda’s experience hosting refugees and argued that the country is offering a practical response to a migration crisis that powerful destination countries have struggled to solve.

The proposal is still under discussion, and France is not a participant. Rwanda is working with Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands on a return hub for people whose asylum claims have been rejected, whose legal appeals are exhausted and who face enforceable return decisions.

The governments hope to begin transfers in 2027. The Netherlands says the first phase would involve single men. It says transferred people would have residence rights and access to education, work, health care and the legal system.

The European countries would cover the costs. Reuters has reported that the pilot could initially accommodate about 100 people at a time, a small number compared with Europe’s wider migration challenge.

Rwanda’s offer may be limited in scale, but it reflects a willingness to share responsibility when many countries have struggled to agree on workable alternatives.

Rwanda’s record gives context to that offer. Since 2019, the country has received thousands of asylum seekers and refugees evacuated from Libya through an emergency arrangement established with the African Union and UNHCR.

Rwanda’s government reported this year that more than 3,000 people had arrived and 2,681 had been resettled in third countries, including 332 in France. The Libya programme is not the same as the proposed European hub.

It was designed to protect people evacuated from dangerous conditions while longer-term solutions were pursued. One early account from Gashora described young Eritreans who had been detained in Libya, now gathered around a table football game and enjoying a freedom they had not known for months.

Rwanda had provided temporary refuge, while other countries, including France, offered places for resettlement.

Rwanda also hosts more than 140,000 refugees and asylum seekers, mainly from the Democratic Republic of Congo and Burundi. Its laws provide for refugees’ access to national services, including education and health care.

At the same time, UNHCR reports that most refugees in Rwanda continue to live in camps. That is a significant part of the picture, but it does not determine how the proposed return hub would be organised.

Its accommodation, legal protections and residents’ freedom of movement will depend on arrangements still being developed.

The country’s welcome to the Afghan girls’ school SOLA after the Taliban returned to power in 2021 offers another vivid example of Rwanda responding to an urgent need. Nearly 250 members of the school community arrived in Rwanda on August 25.

Four days later, classes resumed. The school’s story does not answer every question about the new proposal, but it shows what a welcome can mean in human terms. For the girls, a sudden flight from danger did not have to mean the end of their education.

There was a similar effort to keep Sudanese medical students’ futures from being derailed by war. When fighting closed their university in Khartoum, about 200 students were admitted to the University of Rwanda to continue their studies.

Many were close to completing their medical training. One student, Dina Abdalrahim Obaid, thanked Rwanda for offering “refuge and opportunity to continue our studies.” The welcome was practical as well as symbolic.

The students could continue their curriculum and train in local hospitals, preserving skills they hoped one day to use in Sudan.

Serious questions remain. The plan’s final terms, including the facility’s location and conditions, have not all been made public. UNHCR says it is advising the participating governments on international standards and the protection of people in need.

That involvement should not be described as endorsement. The UK’s earlier Rwanda arrangement also remains part of the debate, although it was different. It proposed transferring asylum seekers while their claims were still to be processed in Rwanda.

In 2023, the UK Supreme Court found that arrangement unlawful on the evidence before it, citing the risk that people could be returned to danger. The new proposal concerns people whose claims have already been rejected, but it will still need clear safeguards and independent scrutiny.

Yet the tone of some Western criticism risks turning a serious policy debate into a familiar lecture directed at an African country. Thevenot’s criticism is especially striking because France is not part of the proposed return hub, while France has accepted hundreds of people resettled through Rwanda’s Libya evacuation programme.

That does not mean French politicians should stay silent, or that Rwanda should be beyond scrutiny. It does, however, make the easy dismissal of Rwanda’s role look selective.

When Rwanda helps shelter people in crisis, the arrangement can be welcomed. When it proposes a new way to share responsibility, it is quickly portrayed as proof of bad faith.

To many in Kigali, that can feel like a form of political blackmail. Rwanda is asked to help manage a crisis Europe has not solved, then its offer is met with sweeping condemnation before the terms have been finalised.

The participating European governments themselves describe the project as a partnership, and the details deserve close examination. Scrutiny should be specific and fair. It should assess the actual safeguards, rather than reduce Rwanda’s role to a caricature or imply that an African country cannot contribute to solving a global problem.

Rwanda is not responsible for creating the migration pressures confronting Europe, yet it has offered to help address them. The proposed hub is not a complete answer, and its success will depend on whether people are treated lawfully and humanely after arrival.

Still, the stories of the Eritrean evacuees in Gashora, the Afghan girls back in class and the Sudanese students continuing their medical training show why Rwanda’s offer deserves more than reflexive suspicion.

Powerful countries have spent years debating migration while dangerous routes and human trafficking persist. Rwanda has stepped forward to share the burden. The safeguards should be tested, but so should the fairness of those judging the country that is willing to help.

MN202611_1sm8s491ol3.t:
The UK has signed an £8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

The five-year deal, awarded to defence firm Babcock, will create 3,000 new jobs and around 2,500 apprentice and graduate roles mainly across Plymouth, Clyde and Bristol, the MoD said.

It will allow the Royal Navy to "work around the clock to get our submarines back out to sea" and see naval base services modernised, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it demonstrated his commitment to "keeping the public safe" and "providing opportunities to "get young people into work".

"We're providing opportunities to get young people into work, to bring jobs to communities in Plymouth, Clyde and beyond, and to boost growth across the UK," the prime minister added.

Streeting said: "We're not going to repeat the mistakes of the past, where investment in our nuclear capability was delayed.

"Even when we have to move funding from other departments, we will prioritise our nuclear deterrent and getting Britain warfighting ready."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast during a visit to HMNB Devonport on Thursday, the defence secretary described the investment as a "win for the Navy… for jobs and the taxpayer."

He said the structure of the contract incentivises Babcock to produce results, adding "the more productive they are, the more they earn but if they fall short, then they don't get paid as much".

Streeting was also asked about reports that 100,000 military reservists who previously served in the armed forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

"What we're doing today is contacting our strategic reserves to make sure their contact details are up to date and we have those details to hand and this is all part of our readiness picture," he said.

The funding is part of a wider £26bn investment into the UK's naval bases announced earlier this year.

First Sea Lord, General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said it will allow the Navy to "tackle delays that hold us back" by "getting submarines through maintenance quicker and back where they belong: beneath the waves".

Harry Holt, Babcock's chief executive, said: "We are very proud at Babcock of the critical support that we provide to the Royal Navy, in particular our unwavering support to the continuous at sea deterrent – the UK's highest defence priority."
