MN202611_hnykgkrgxe.t:
Jordan said they were taken to a sports court on the Etihad campus and were told they would not be able to leave

Some Don Toliver fans who were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live arena after an unknown substance was released have said they were "quarantined for six hours" and threatened with arrest if they did not remove all their clothing.

Jordan, 33, from Scotland, said he and his brothers were among 88 people who were taken for decontamination after the incident at the gig on Sunday night , and it "felt like I was being taken hostage".

He said they had asked for medical help at 22:15 GMT and were taken to the Etihad Stadium, where they were made to change into paper suits, and stayed until 04:45 on Monday.

"It was so traumatic," Jordan said. Greater Manchester Police declined to comment.

The force has not confirmed what the substance was and there have been no arrests.

A woman was taken to hospital, with 88 other people reporting symptoms, including coughing and chest pains.

Dry decontamination was carried out by North West Ambulance Service (NWAS), GMP said.

NWAS said it had deployed crews, including its Hazardous Area Response Team, who carried out decontamination "as a precaution" in line with "advice taken from national scientific advisors based on the situation".

Concertgoers said they were held for hours and asked to strip after an evacuation at Co-op Live

Jordan said his 15-year-old brother first approached police officers for help when they all started to develop symptoms 15 minutes after the incident.

"Our eyes started to feel like one sensation and then we started to feel like chest pains and coughs," he said.

"We went there for help, they obviously knew that they were keeping people there, but they never told us, 'once you're in you can't get out'.

Three hours later - at about 01:30 on Monday - Jordan said the fire service told concertgoers that they would have to remove their clothes before being taken in a van to another area of Etihad Campus.

According to NHS England guidance , external , dry decontamination - the use of a dry material to remove a contaminant - should be the "default intervention" for anyone suspected of being contaminated in a chemical incident.

The guidance also suggests patients should "remove outer clothing if affected by the substance".

Jordan said he was initially told he would not have his clothes returned for two weeks

"They said we had to strip down, clothes off, put paper overalls on and then we had to get moved into a quarantine area which was across the road," Jordan said.

Jordan claimed when he expressed concern to police officers, who were also based inside the sports hall, and asked why they needed to remove their clothes he was threatened with arrest.

"They said if I didn't commit to the decontamination, I would be arrested and charged for breach of the peace," he said.

Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service have also been approached for comment.

About 70 quarantined concertgoers were allegedly held for more than six hours before being released

In a previous statement, GMFRS said crews had been in attendance for about seven hours "to ensure the safety of every person attending the event".

GMP said 88 people were "accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed".

Jordan said that at about 04:45 an officer told them that if they gave their details they would be able to go.

Archie Grime, from Accrington, said he was sitting "doing nothing for hours" during the quarantine

"We received our clothes and shoes, but we were not allowed to put them back on, he said.

"We had to walk back to the hotel in socks and the paper gown in the freezing cold."

Jordan said he and his two brothers were both receiving further medical treatment after being advised to attend hospital in Scotland.

A group of friends from Scunthorpe, Molly, 19, Kyan 22, Charlie, 20, and Jack, 21, said they were also "up all night" during the decontamination process.

They said it was "confusing" and there was not much information about what was happening and why.

Friends Molly, 19, Kyan 22, Charlie, 20, and Jack, 21, were all "up all night" while the decontamination happened

Molly, 19, said she was separated from her friends due to her gender which made her feel "alone".

"We were allowed a screen around us, it was all women in there, we had to literally strip down to our bra and knickers and put on a suit and slippers," she said.

"We had to put [our clothes] in a plastic bag and it got taken away.

"We were told 'I hope you've not got anything expensive as you might not get it back'."

She added: "There was no ABC of what was happening. It was just, 'you have to take your clothes off' but there was no further information."

Charlie said: "It was invasive, you had to wipe yourself down, wipe down your phone.

"Everything goes in a bag, But it was a mystery. No-one was telling us what was going to happen."

At about 04:30 the friends said they were given their clothes back and they were able to leave.

College student Archie Grime, 18, from Accrington, Lancashire, said he was also quarantined after the concert.

"It was burning and painful and I couldn't see or breathe," he said.

He said he and his friends sat "doing nothing for hours" while waiting to be released.

Archie said when the group were told they could leave the Etihad, he was able to get a lift home - but noted others were left "stranded" without transport plans.

"A friend's mum took us home," he said. "We were lucky though, a lot of people were stranded.

"They told us to walk back in the thin suits in the cold and to take our clothes home to be washed."

Police said the cordon was lifted at Co-op Live on Tuesday night, as the investigation continues.

The force said the substance release may be linked to robberies and stolen jewellery at the venue.

MN202611_16ccjys5gfm.t:
The book is described as a "cheeky treat" filled with "charm and imagination"

A father and son have won the Waterstones Children's Book of the Year after being inspired as they enjoyed an arts and crafts evening at home.

Dan Ojari and his eight-year-old son Finn, from Bristol, created Is This a Plum? after "drawing, thinking and laughing" about what some shapes look like.

Ojari said he realised that "a plum looks a lot like a hippo's bum" and it led to the pair creating a book filled with "visual tricks and rhyming reveals".

Waterstones head of books Bea Carvalho described Is This a Plum? as "picture-book perfection". She said it was "endlessly re-readable, a cheeky treat for little ones, with plenty of nostalgia appeal for grown-ups".

The playful rhyming book featuring interactive cut-outs was among 20 recommended books on the Waterstones shortlist.

The book features shapes which readers use to guess what is on the next page

Dan Ojari works at Aardman Animations and enjoys drawing with his two sons.

He said he hoped the book would make readers smile and think and, above all, "sit down and chuckle with your family and friends".

Finn has been an artist for most of his life but he said that he hoped to one day become a "real-life wizard".

He said Is It A Plum? was "very easy to read and will probably make you laugh at least once".

The father and son duo said they wanted to inspire children to start "drawing, writing and making things to share with the world".

MN202611_15ro8n9h543.t:
A surge in severe cases of flu has prompted health officials in England to urge those most at risk to get vaccinated as soon as possible.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said hospital admission rates had soared by almost 80% over the last week to the highest at this time of year since before the Covid pandemic.

Flu vaccine uptake so far among those aged 65 and over is just under 68% - lower than where it usually is at this time of year, the agency said. The flu can be very serious for those living with some long term health conditions.

Outgoing chief executive for NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, said how some hospitals have introduced mask-wearing to stem the spread of respiratory illnesses.

Winter flu vaccine rollout begins. Who's eligible?

Are max strength cold and flu pills worth the money?

Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".

"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.

However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.

Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles – whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it.

UKHSA flu lead Dr Suzanna McDonald told the BBC that the sharp rise in flu cases was happening earlier compared to last winter and previous flu seasons.

"Flu is very, very unpredictable and we don't know what the flu season will look like until it has unfolded," she said, adding that although last year's flu season arrived early, it peaked at "moderate levels".

She said it is not known if this flu season will go on for longer, or peak higher, but urged people to get vaccinated, saying said thousands of people die from the flu every year.

However, flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practice good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 37% of those eligible have taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies until 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives".

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

MN202611_c8xpk3toxt.t:
Marco Rose replaced Andoni Iraola - who ended up at Liverpool - in the summer

Bournemouth are dreaming of winning the Europa League after staging a 10-man fightback to join a select band of teams to win their first five European games.

The Cherries trailed 1-0 to Iago Aspas' goal at Celta Vigo, and then went down to 10 men midway through the first half when Bafode Diakite was sent off.

But second-half goals from Alvaro Rodriguez and Rayan gave the Cherries a 10th consecutive win in all competitions, extending their club record run.

Bournemouth are only the third side to win each of their first five European matches (excluding qualifiers and including the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup), after Nuremberg in 1961-62 and Ararat in 1972-73.

They top this season's table as the only club to win five out of five - and are closing in on a top-eight spot, which would mean they skip a play-off round and go straight into the last 16.

Some fans have told the BBC they have already booked hotels in Frankfurt for the final on 26 May.

As supporters sang about reaching that game, midfielder Alex Scott was asked for his thoughts on TNT Sports.

"Of course that's our dream. When you grow up wanting to be a footballer you dream of winning trophies," Scott said.

"Where this club has come from to where it is now, full credit to everyone who has built it.

"For players, it's a dream to be on the pitch playing for this club. We have still got wins to get to qualify into the top eight, and from there all focus is on pushing forward and hopefully we can go on and win it."

The Cherries are in unprecedented times, with their biggest trophy to date being when they won the second-tier Championship in 2014-15.

In terms of cups, they won the 1983–84 Associate Members' Cup - which later became the EFL Trophy.

Head coach Marco Rose, who replaced Andoni Iraola in the summer, said: "It's always allowed to dream.

"If you get a competition like this you want to achieve the best possible thing. We know it's far away to go. Many games. Now it's about getting into the top eight to avoid more games and then we can see step by step."

As well as just winning their games, Bournemouth are firing in the goals. They have netted at least twice in each match during this 10-game winning run.

And they are the first side to score at least twice in each of their first five matches in Europe since Queens Park Rangers in 1976.

The win on Thursday was made even more impressive by the fact they contested 75% of the game with 10 men.

It came days after Manchester United seemed to implode after an early red card against Liverpool , losing 4-0.

Former England manager Glenn Hoddle said on TNT: "They have deserved this result. They've played beautifully with 10 men - probably as good as I've seen a team play defensively and with the ball.

"I've not seen a team go down to 10 men for so long and dictate a game and deserve to win the game. They were absolutely brilliant."

Cherries boss Rose told BBC Radio Solent: "What a team, what a spirit, what an energy.

"I said to Ty [Tyler Adams] sometimes it's not about tactics and formations and stuff like this. [David] Brooks did a great job when we got one player less - he played right defender like he played it for 10 years. We changed in the right moment. Everyone did his job on a really high level.

"We were just relentless and we never stopped to believe in this win and that's why big, big, big congratulations to the team.

"You feel if you're one player down that it's a difficult night, but to handle a difficult night like this, it just shows the character of the team and of the whole group."

The coach's belief in what they are doing filters through to the players.

Amine Adli, who set up the equaliser, told the BBC: "At half-time, everyone still believed we can turn the game in our way and this is what happened.

"Everyone was like 'guys we can make it, we have to believe. If we score the game can change.'"

Earlier this month, the attacking midfielder said he saw a lot of similarities to the Bayer Leverkusen team he was part of in 2023-24.

That is not a bad comparison, considering they went unbeaten to win the domestic double, as well as reaching the Europa League final.

So who can blame the Cherries for dreaming?

MN202611_1dz2iq2vf6w.t:
Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?

Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.

Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.

Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.

The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.

From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.

In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.

That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.

For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants.

It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC.

That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ.

"The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports".

Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island.

To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors.

On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain.

Data centres worth billions of dollars are being built in Malaysia

It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics.

"Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says.

In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to market research group CBRE , external . The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025.

In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States.

But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy.

The world's biggest tech firms - Google, Microsoft, Oracle - also plan to boost their spending on infrastructure in the region by roughly 60% this year, CBRE added.

The demand for neoclouds, which are specialised data centres which power AI, has also risen rapidly, it said.

For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC.

In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation.

In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story.

Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open."

However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better.

Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China.

Those efforts seem to have been renewed. Just last week, Washington announced new rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The latest move not only restricts the export of high-end chips to China, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train AI models.

Jensen Huang signs a Taiwanese banknote for a visitor at Computex 2026 in Taipei

This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment.

Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang.

Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks.

"Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank.

Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets.

Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat.

Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry.

"I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said.

"The story is not over yet... Jensen coming back is probably the biggest, baddest return ever. The question is what will happen next?"

MN202611_e9sh9wldqq.t:
Shauna said the future had been "ripped apart" after her partner, Row, was diagnosed with very severe ME

Rowena Davies had been planning to travel the world with her partner until an ME diagnosis left her unable to talk or leave her bed.

The 42-year-old, known as Row, initially thought she was burnt out, but after years of searching for answers was finally diagnosed in 2021 and her partner Shauna Chambers has since given up work to help the family care for her.

Campaigners are warning that people with severe ME - sometimes referred to clinically as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome - could die without changes to services in Wales.

The Welsh government said proposals for an all‑Wales specialist, an expert group and national standards were being considered.

It is estimated more than 400,000 people across the UK have ME, a complex multi-system condition with no known cure.

Shauna, 34, said: "She had a cough that didn't leave for many months, but the main thing was that she would be absolutely drained and exhausted after doing such small things.

"Now, she really isn't able to do anything at all."

Row loves being outdoors but she's now been in bed for five years

Shauna, from Tywyn in Gwynedd, said Row was "full of energy" and loved sport, but now she cannot tolerate light or noise, and any exertion will cause her to deteriorate.

"We feed her, we wash her, we brush her teeth. We were left to navigate this on our own," she said.

"It's like you're grieving someone that is still alive, and you sit next to her sometimes, and all you can do is just hold her hand and breathe.

"People's lives have been completely ruined by this condition, and if nothing changes people can die from ME, and it is absolutely avoidable."

Campaigners told BBC Wales in March that healthcare services were "like a desert" for those most severely affected.

Shauna has been campaigning on behalf of her partner and other patients in Wales

With the right support, Row's family are hopeful she can get better. She recently had her first visit by the Living Well service within Betsi Cadwaladr health board, which has been expanded to include ME, and now aims to support people living with any severity of the condition.

It uses funding from the Welsh government's Adferiad programme , external but campaigners say that services vary between health boards. There is no clinical lead for ME in Wales.

John Peters has lived with ME for more than 40 years

John Peters, 65, from Swansea, was diagnosed with the condition 40 years ago. He was once a keen rugby player, but after a virus, his life changed.

"I would rest for a couple of days which would sort of take the edge off it, and then I'd sort of go at it again, and it would make it worse," he explained.

He now describes the effects as being mild to moderate, but he has spent periods of his life lying in a dark room for days on end.

"I've gone through improvements, and then got another infection, and that's been the cycle of my life since 1985," he said.

"One of the hardest things is the loss of identity. You're not a husband, a father, you don't have a career.

"Your life goes past and then you realise what's happened. I hate the illness.

"No one knows what I've been through. There is no care for me."

Swansea Bay University Health Board said its service, also funded by the Adferiad programme, "focuses on improving quality of life, supporting independence, and enabling individuals to manage the impact of ME within their own daily circumstances" while "recognising the fluctuating nature of the condition and the importance of personalised care".

ME is a chronic and complex multi-system condition, which causes symptoms such as extreme fatigue and post-exertional malaise.

That means simple physical or mental activities can leave people completely debilitated.

Not everyone with ME is affected in the same way. There is a spectrum of severity, which is often categorised as mild, moderate, severe and very severe.

While researchers are still investigating the causes, triggers may include infection or other illness. There is no specific treatment.

Liverpool-based private consultant Dr Binita Kane, who has a special interest in ME and long Covid, said she had a growing waiting list of patients across the UK.

"I think that is a sad reflection on the fact that the services, sadly, don't exist at the moment in the way they need to through the NHS," she said.

"Even if patients can access a service, they often can't access medications and treatments for symptom control and support for overlapping conditions because there aren't doctors integrated into those services."

She said the goal is always "to prevent people from getting into the very severe state" through early intervention, but she said that certain investigations can happen at people's homes, such as 24-hour ECG tests, sleep studies and blood tests.

"People sadly do die from severe ME for different reasons, it is a risk, and ME is one of the only conditions I'm aware of where the more sick you are, the less access to treatment and help and support you get," she added.

"These are young people whose lives have been decimated, destroyed, who aren't getting enough help, care, and support.

"There's a million reasons why the government should be taking this extremely seriously."

Sonya Chowdhury of Action for ME said patients had been "waiting too long" for changes to services

Campaign groups in Wales have joined together to call on the government to bring together a national expert group, appoint an all-Wales clinical lead, and develop a research strategy.

In a recent survey of more than 5,400 people across the UK, 62.1% of respondents in Wales reported having no NHS specialist ME service in their area, compared with 32.8% in England.

Action for ME, who conducted the survey, said the findings demonstrate that "access to specialist care remains a postcode lottery".

"People have been waiting for decades and that is too long" said the charity's chief executive Sonya Chowdhury.

She said that a cross-party debate was held in the Senedd in December 2025 in which the current health minister, Plaid Cymru's Mabon ap Gwynfor MS, advocated on behalf of ME patients while in opposition.

"We are 12 months on, and we are yet to see action," she added.

"It's fantastic that the minister has met with us and other groups here in Wales, and we have heard some positive noises, but what we need to see now is something changing."

A Welsh government spokesperson said it's "working to improve support for people living with post-infection associated chronic illness, including ME, and recognise that more needs to be done".

"We have met with groups representing people with ME and long Covid. We aim to provide an update in due course," it added.

"Through Adferiad, we provide £8m a year to develop services and specialist clinical expertise to support people with long-term conditions, including ME."

MN202611_5bmix4ffdy.t:
Volunteers from local communities have been involved in setting out the plants

Floating islands are being installed on ponds in five of Glasgow's parks as part of the 2026 Commonwealth Games legacy.

The islands, which are being planted by community groups, are designed to encourage wildlife and help clean the water.

The project will create almost 250 square metres of new wildlife habitat which is expected to last about 20 years.

Glasgow 2026 organisers say they are funding the projects as part of their commitment to greener games.

Ellen Hebdon says the plants' roots play an important role in preventing and removing harmful algae from the water

The islands are manufactured by a Moray-based company which has been exporting them around the world.

Biomatrix Water Solutions in Forres has installed islands in Boston, Venice and London.

They have also been floated onto the River Clyde at the Glasgow Science Centre as part of an unrelated project.

The new islands are being installed at Victoria Park, Elder Park, Richmond Park, Queen's Park and Hogganfield Loch.

Ellen Hebdon, the company's operations manager, said the plants' roots played an important role in preventing and removing harmful algae from the water.

"It's not an overnight solution, but over a period of time, you will see benefits in the clarity and the cleanliness of the water," she said.

Floating islands have been installed at the Glasgow Science Centre

The islands are made up of recycled plastic materials, including drinking water pipes, to create buoyancy and are held together using marine-grade stainless steel.

They are then topped with a lightweight clay aggregate, called leca, into which the plants are inserted.

The aquatic plants include a mix of evergreen and flowering native species such as marsh marigolds, water forget-me-nots and ragged robin.

Their roots underneath the islands provide shelter for aquatic wildlife.

The location, in the middle of the water, also provides nesting spaces for birds, which would be largely free from disturbance.

Local schools and "friends of the park" groups are helping with the planting and maintenance.

Games organisers say sustainability is an important delivery factor with all competition venues powered by renewable electricity and electric or hybrid vehicles making up two thirds of the transport fleet.

Glasgow 2026's head of sustainability, Selina Donald, said the city council had been looking at creating floating islands but did not have the funding.

"I really saw the pride in all the parks, the pride in the green spaces, the pride in the natural environment across the city," she said. "And so really, for us, it was a way that we can celebrate and support that."

MN202611_1a0rpjtkm0n.t:
Watch: Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine's president also said it was "very strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like hugging Adolf Hitler during WWII.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it wasn't clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .

Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the strikes, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without coordinating with its partners.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent strikes on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They've also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

MN202611_dup79sl6ni.t:
Simone Magill made her return to football as a late substitute for Birmingham City against Manchester United on Sunday

After 13 months away, Simone Magill made her return to football as a late substitute in Birmingham City's WSL defeat by Manchester United on Sunday.

It was a moment that had been a long time coming for the 31-year-old, who gave birth to her daughter, Skye, in May and has been building towards stepping back on the pitch.

Now, she will hope to make her international return with Northern Ireland in a friendly against Greece on Friday.

"It's been some time since I've been here in a playing capacity, so it's really nice just to be back in the mix again," NI captain Magill told BBC Sport NI.

"I officially made my comeback at the weekend and it was really nice to have done that. I'm really looking forward to doing that here at home in front of the fans and my family as well."

'You can be a mum and a footballer - they can co-exist'

Greece friendlies an opportunity to build - Andrews

In an interview with BBC Sport in October, Magill spoke about how being both a mum and a footballer can "co-exist".

While she was not ready to play any role in the matches, Magill, Skye and her husband Mark were all in camp for the World Cup play-off with Portugal last month, all with an eye of integrating into international duty as a family.

Having played just a handful of minutes, Northern Ireland manager Michael McArdle said that while he was "delighted" to have Magill back, how much she plays across the double-header would be in collaboration with Birmingham and his captain.

"With the circumstances around this one, I'm very mindful that I need to build accordingly and I really need to listen to myself as well," Magill added.

"To even be back in this capacity this soon after giving birth, for me, is just unbelievable.

"I have no major expectations. I'm just really happy to be here and be a part of it, and if I do come on, that'll be even better."

Watch live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport app and website

Friday's match against Greece will be Northern Ireland's first friendly in three years.

The sides will then play again on Tuesday at 16:00 GMT, and both matches can be streamed live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport app and website.

The matches will act as preparation for the Nations League campaign in February, when Northern Ireland face tricky tests in the form of Poland, Finland and Belarus.

McArdle is developing a young squad and Magill says she hopes to bring "leadership and experience to really help us all move forward".

"We've obviously had a transition in the last year whilst I've been out, it's been nice to come back in and just feel where we're at, get on the grass with the girls and see, 'how can I help, what can I bring?'," she added.

"I'm very much looking forward to just getting back in the mix and helping try to bring the young players forward, use that experience and let's hold on to the ball, let's get into the final third, let's have a go, be brave - all of the attributes that we're known for.

"We're an underdog nation, so it's getting that across to the younger members in the squad to say, 'let's have a go with these teams and not be afraid'."

Simone Magill (centre) is set to make her Northern Ireland return against Greece

In her absence over the past year, Northern Ireland have used a number of different options in the centre forward role.

Winger Lauren Wade has shown her versatility by playing centrally, while Kess Elmore and Cora Chambers have also played up top.

Along with Magill, Portsmouth striker Kerry Beattie is also back in the squad to bolster McArdle's striking options.

"We've loads of young ones snapping at my heels. It's great, that's what we want.

"I feel we're more competitive now than ever. You never know who's going to be coming into the squad. Certainly, in more recent years, you kind of knew the squad every single time, whereas that's not the case now.

"We've got some exciting youth coming through, so it's their time now to shine."

Magill added that Northern Ireland are "heading in a new direction" ahead of the Nations League campaign next year, and the friendlies with Greece give an opportunity for the team to grow in a pressure-free environment.

"We're coming into a brand new campaign and it's really nice that we have a friendly window just now.

"We haven't had one in a very, very long time, so this is a brilliant opportunity to get us all back together, get the new faces in, get some more experience, learn things, try things.

"I'm really excited about where we're going."

MN202611_1lhmjnmfg4g.t:
The UK has agreed the deals in a bit to cut red tape for British companies

The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.

The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.

The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.

But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".

"The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".

He added: "European economies are not growing as fast as ours. The idea that getting closer to the EU will mean growth for us is a myth."
